newsitem.title: USA: Clinton hails drop in out-of-wedlock births.
newsitem.headline: Clinton hails drop in out-of-wedlock births.

text.p: President Clinton released his weekly radio address a day early Friday to take credit for new data showing that the out-of-wedlock birth rate fell last year for the first time in 19 years.

Clinton, who has secluded himself in western New York state to prepare for Sunday's presidential debate with Republican Bob Dole, took the unusual step of distributing the text of his Saturday radio address ahead of time to draw attention to the figures and to use them to buttress his pro-family campaign message.
A division of the Atlanta-based Centres for Disease Control and Prevention reported that the birth rate for unmarried women of all ages fell by 4 percent in 1995, its first decline since 1976.
It also said the teenage birth rate had decreased by an estimated 3 percent in 1995 from 1994, marking the fourth consecutive annual decline.

Under ordinary circumstances, the numbers might be of interest mostly to public health officials, but with the Nov. 5 election looming, they quickly became fodder for the president's re-election campaign.
"When the teen birth rate drops for four years in a row and out-of-wedlock births decline for the first time in a generation, that is news we can all be proud of," Clinton said in the radio address.
"There are still far too many children being born outside of marriage, but we are now finally seeing that it is possible for us to move in the right direction," he added.
The Dole campaign fired back quickly, blasting Clinton for not making teen drug use an equal priority.

"If Clinton is taking credit for reducing teen pregnancy, then he must also accept blame for the massive increase in teen drug use under his watch," Dole's deputy press secretary Christina Martin said in a statement.
"It's time to elect a president who will show moral leadership in every area, not just the ones that make his poll numbers go up," she said.

In the address, Clinton sought to portray his policies, including requiring young mothers to stay in school or lose their welfare benefits and a crackdown on parents who do not make child support payments, as contributing to the declines.

"We believe that the tough message about parental responsibility ... and putting a concentrated focus on this from the bully pulpit has helped generate the right climate for this improvement," White House spokesman Mike McCurry said.
